items.text: To develop an understanding of how knowledge is created, evaluated, refined and changed within biology.
To enable students to understand and use the vocabulary, structures and forms of expression which characterize the study of biology.
To develop students' abilities to access knowledge.
Understand the nature of the study of biology.
Examine the types of questions which biologists investigate.
Exhibit a curiosity about life and the conditions which support life.
Appreciate the nature of scientific investigations and the findings of science.
Recognize the relationship between what is studied in biology and daily life.
Define the term biology.
Use a microscope to examine cells.
Develop proper techniques for handling and care of a microscope.
View prepared slides.
Prepare wet-mount slides.
Sketch what is seen in the field of view.
Estimate sizes of objects observed.
Compare the images produced by light microscopes and electron microscopes.
Discuss examples of how the microscope has altered what we know.
Explain the importance of theory in biology.
Outline the key aspects of a scientific theory. (See the Unit Overview and web.)
Discuss the development of the cell theory.
Recognize the link between the development of cell theory and the technology available to study cells.
Realize the significance of cell theory in establishing the relatedness of all living organisms.
Examine the principles of natural selection as identified by Darwin and Wallace.
Explain how natural selection is the basis of the theory of evolution.
Describe how a theory might change using an example(s).

units.name: Ecological Organization
factorsEmphasized: D3 impact of science and technology
D4 science, technology, and the environment
D8 limitations of science and technology
D9 social influence on science and technology
D11 science, technology and other realms
F3 search for data and their meaning

items.text: To strengthen students' knowledge and understanding of how to compute, measure, estimate and interpret numerical data, when to apply these skills and techniques, and why these processes apply to the study of populations.
To develop an understanding of how knowledge is created, evaluated, refined, and changed within biology.
To promote intuitive, imaginative thought and the ability to evaluate ideas, processes, experiences and objects in the context of the study of the environment.
To enable students to understand and use the vocabulary, structures and forms of expression which characterize the study of ecology.
To support the development of a positive disposition to life-long learning.
To support students in coming to a better understanding of the personal, moral, social, and cultural aspects of the study of life.
To develop an understanding that technology both shapes society and is shaped by society.
Explain how the interactions among the soil, climate, and living organisms produce the ecosystems which can be observed.
Identify the components of soil.
Describe the soil types of Saskatchewan.
Determine how soil characteristics influence plant growth.
Describe how climatic variations in Saskatchewan influence plant growth.
Investigate variations in plant growth on slopes.
Identify some soil microorganisms.
Discuss the importance of soil microorganisms.
Appreciate that the soil and the climate are the keys to life in Saskatchewan, and on this planet.
Investigate the interrelationship of agriculture and the environment.
Discuss the following cycles and attempt to illustrate their interrelationship: water, carbon dioxide-oxygen, nitrogen.
Analyze a variety of ecosystems.
Understand the concept of niche and habitat.
Identify the biotic and abiotic components and interactions in the ecosystems observed.
Describe how the human community is dependent on the soil, water, and air.
Formulate some food chains and webs involving the human community.
Describe how the human community in which one lives is dependent on, and influenced by, the climate.
Identify both symbiotic and competitive relationships among organisms within a community.
Investigate a natural community in the neighbourhood of the school.
Compare the similarities and differences between the natural community and the constructed/human community.
Compare communities which have other soil types or other climate types.
Discuss succession in communities.
Identify how human activity, e.g. agriculture and urbanization, has altered succession or changed its rate.
Indicate some determiners of succession.
Describe life in past ecosystems.
Examine the evidence of life in the past.
Debate change and extinction theories.
Investigate the role of humans in creating and sustaining conditions which alter the rate of ecological change.
Explain how populations are counted.
Recall the criteria which define a population.
Identify some populations of plants or animals in the local area.
Describe methods of estimation by sampling.
Estimate some populations using one or more methods.
Analyze population changes.
Identify factors which influence reproduction rates and death rates.
Recognize factors which affect immigration and emigration.
Compare cyclic populations and stable populations.
Discuss the carrying capacity of planet Earth for the human population.
Recognize ecological sequencing.
Identify the sequencing present in the following terms: biosphere, biome, ecosystem, community, and population.
Review several examples of biomes by discussing some of their major kinds of plants.
Draw a climatogram and discuss temperature and moisture as major determiners of a specific ecological area.

units.name: The Diversity of Life
factorsEmphasized: D2 scientists and technologists are human
F3 search for data and their meaning

items.text: To develop an understanding of how knowledge is created, evaluated, refined, and changed within biology.
To use a wide range of possibilities for developing students' knowledge of the major concepts within biology.
To support the development of a positive disposition to life-long learning.
To develop compassionate, empathetic and fair-minded students who can make positive contributions to society as individuals and as members of groups.
Describe the principles of classification.
Discuss everyday examples of classification. (Then discuss the value of having a biological classification and some of the unique problems that might manifest themselves.)
Compare several different ways organisms are grouped into kingdoms. (It would be useful to have the students see the historical development of the 5 kingdom structure from a 2 kingdom structure.)
Understand the system of binomial nomenclature. (Discuss the 7 major classification units which include Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, and Species and their associated relationships.)
Use dichotomous keys to help identify organisms. (One could demonstrate that a key locates actual organisms just as binomial nomenclature and the species level identifies actual organisms.)
Recognize the role of monera, protists, and fungi in the ecosystem.
Describe viral structure and activity.
Identify some viral diseases prevalent in plants, animals, and humans in Saskatchewan.
Discuss the various ways bacteria are classified.
Describe some diseases caused by bacteria which affect organisms living in Saskatchewan.
Identify some valuable roles played in the ecosystem by bacteria.
Distinguish between prokaryotes and eukaryotes.
Describe how the protist kingdom is classified.
Collect, culture, and observe a variety of protists.
Describe the general characteristics of fungi.
Collect and observe some samples of fungi.
Identify the basic structural features of bacteria.
Describe the diversity of plants.
Compare nonvascular and vascular plants.
Identify, describe, and collect some examples of nonvascular and vascular plants.
Discuss the ways that vascular plants are classified.
Describe grain crops and forage crops grown in Saskatchewan. (Correlate with Unit 20-4.)
Chart the ranges of representative plants of Saskatchewan.
Recognize the diversity of animals.

Describe the characteristics of the major animal phyla. (It is suggested that the teacher consider a mollusk such as a clam or snail, an annelid such as an earthworm, an arthropod such as an insect or spider, and one or more of the chordates, as time allows, which would include a mammal.)
Identify members of each phylum which contains animals native to Saskatchewan.
Describe the habitat and niche of animals native to Saskatchewan.
Contrast innate behaviour in animals with learned behaviour.
Describe social behaviour in animals.

printedNotes.text: Note: Objective 1.8 should be seen as a general organizer and is not intended to be used to rigorously cover great detail on plant tissues.

items.text: To promote both intuitive, imaginative thought and the ability to evaluate ideas, processes, experiences, and objects within the context of the study of ecosystems.
To use a wide range of possibilities for developing students' knowledge of the major concepts within biology.
To develop students' abilities to meet their own learning needs.
To support students in coming to a better understanding of the personal, moral, social, and cultural aspects of the study of life.
Recognize the various biological processes associated with plant systems.
Compare sexual and asexual reproduction in angiosperms.
Describe the processes of pollen production, fertilization and seed formation of plants.
Describe the means by which solutions are transported through plants.
Investigate the environmental and biological influences on growth.
Describe the major plant systems of various cereal, oilseed, pulse, forage, or native crops.
Identify the effects of climate and pest on different stages of crop development.
Review the three major structures of a plant which include the root, stem and leaf along with their locations and functions.

Identify four broad tissue areas found in a plant which include meristematic, protective, vascular and fundamental.
• meristematic: frequent mitotic division for growth which includes cambium.
• protective: epidermis and cuticle.
• vascular: conducts water and minerals (xylem and phloem).
• fundamental tissue: three functions which include food storage, food production and support. (Examples include sclerenchyma, collenchyma and parenchyma. If you use these terms, discuss the Greek/Latin origins and help students make these connections.)
Appreciate the relation of Saskatchewan's biogeographical regions and agricultural activity.
Identify the characteristics of all the biogeographical regions of Saskatchewan.
Compare kinds of grain and forage crops.
Discuss the reasons and issues associated with various land uses and crop diversity.
Identify various species of trees, shrubs, plants and grasses of Saskatchewan.
Compare such plant characteristics as reproduction and growth patterns as they relate to the Saskatchewan environment.
Describe the internal and external influences on plant growth.
Describe the function and effect of cytokinins, auxins, and gibberelins.
Contrast tropisms with responses due to changes in turgor pressure.
Investigate how plants respond to chemicals such as fertilizers and herbicides.
Examine the effect on soil of the application of fertilizers and biofertilizers.
Identify the impact and examples of soil degradation.
Recognize the interconnectedness of agriculture and the environment.
Describe the impact of agriculture on the local environment.
Identify local and global issues associated with agriculture.
Appreciate the complexity of issues such as soil degradation, world hunger and environmental concerns.

units.name: The Chemical Basis of Life
factorsEmphasized: D3 impact of science and technology

items.text: To develop an understanding of how knowledge is created, evaluated, refined, and changed within biology.
To enable students to understand and use the vocabulary, structures and forms of expression which characterize the study of science.
To develop students' abilities to access knowledge.
Appreciate the basic principles of chemistry which are involved in life processes.
Recognize that organisms are made of atoms.
Realize the relationship between the electron structure of atoms and the type of bond which forms.
Understand the relationship between chemical bonds and stored energy.
Recognize the importance and ongoing nature of various chemical reactions in the body.
Discuss a chemical reaction — the reactants, products and energy either required or produced.
Illustrate with examples the similarities and differences between synthesis and decomposition reactions.
Describe some relationships which exist between synthesis and decomposition reactions in relation to the functioning of the body ie., dynamic balance (homeostasis).
Investigate the properties of carbohydrates, lipids, and proteins.
Explain how carbon-based molecules interact with each other through hydrogen bonding.
Compare mono-, di-, and polysaccharides and then provide examples of their usefulness to a living system.
Describe the relationship between fatty acids and fats by providing examples to illustrate when they are useful to a living system.
Describe the relationship between amino acids and proteins with reference to the peptide bond.

Discuss enzymes using a series of key words which should be included in a concept web with the heading of proteins. (The key words are substrate, enzyme—substrate complex, lock and key, catalyst, factors affecting enzyme activity [temperature; relative concentration of substrate], enzymes, and coenzymes.)
Indicate the component parts of a fat molecule.
Recognize the value of proteins by using examples from the human body.
Describe the structure of nucleic acids.
Describe the similarities and differences in the structure of DNA and RNA.
Describe the processes of replication and transcription.

units.name: Cell Structure and Function
factorsEmphasized: E3 using equipment safely page for expla abou see s 81-82 an nation t webs.

items.text: To promote both intuitive, imaginative thought and the ability to evaluate ideas, processes, experiences, and objects within the context of the study of ecosystems.
To use a wide range of possibilities for developing students' knowledge of the major concepts within biology.
To develop students' abilities to meet their own learning needs.
To support the development of a positive disposition to life-long learning.
To develop an understanding that technology both shapes society and is shaped by society.
Describe the structures and functions of cell components.
Review evidence for the existence of cells.
Observe, sketch, and describe a representative sampling of plant and animal cells.
Describe the structure of a cell membrane.
Describe the functions of the organelles found in eukaryotic cells.
Contrast the structure of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.
Explain how the processes of diffusion, active transport, photosynthesis, and respiration are accomplished in a cell.
Identify the factors which influence the rate and direction of diffusion.

Examine the mechanisms of active transport by identifying and explaining the two processes. (Process one involves the expenditure of energy where a carrier molecule takes a substance from one side of a membrane to the other side of the membrane. Process two involves the inpocketing of material by a membrance -- pinocytosis and exocytosis.)
Recognize how the ATP-ADP system, and the NAD-NADH system, transfer energy within a cell.
Compare aerobic and anaerobic metabolism.
Describe the processes involved in photosynthesis and then compare the process of photosynthesis with respiration.
Examine how the structure of the leaf is adapted for the processes involved in photosynthesis.
Identify how osmosis is related to diffusion and the value of osmosis to living organisms.
Compare the similarities and differences between active and passive transport.
Indicate the importance of the light and dark reactions in the process of photosynthesis.

units.name: Genetics
factorsEmphasized: D2 scientists and technologists are human
D3 impact of science and technology
D6 resources for science and technology
D9 social influence on science and technology
D11 science, technology, and other realms

items.text: To enable students to understand and use the vocabulary, structure and forms of expression which characterize the study of biology.
To develop a contemporary view of technology.
To develop an understanding that technology both shapes society and is shaped by society.
To support the development of a positive disposition to life-long learning.
To contribute to the development of "strong sense" critical and creative thinkers.
To develop compassionate, empathetic and fair-minded students who can make positive contributions to society as individuals and as members of groups.
Explain the significance of Mendel's experiments and observations, and the laws derived from them.
Explain the concept of independent events.
Understand that the probability of an independent event is not altered by the outcomes of previous events.
Describe Mendel's experiments and observations.
Describe the relationship between genotype and phenotype.
Use the concept of the gene to explain Mendel's laws.
Describe the ideas of dominant and recessive traits with examples.
Consider the value of the punnett square by creating examples of mono and dihybrid crosses.
Explain the law of segregation.
Discuss the relationships among chromosomes, genes, and DNA.
Describe how the genetic code is carried on the DNA.
Outline the process of replication.
Compare mitosis and meiosis.
Describe the process of transcription.
Describe the functions of mRNA, tRNA, amino acids, and ribosomes in protein synthesis.
Describe the causes and effects of both chromosome and gene mutations.
Consider the purposes and techniques of gene mapping.
Examine incomplete dominance, alleles, sex determination, and sex-linked traits in the context of human genetics.
Discuss several human genetic disorders such as hemophilia, sickle-cell anemia, Down's syndrome, and Tay-Sach's disease.
Discuss the similarities and differences between sex chromosomes and somatic chromosomes.
Using examples from living organisms discuss the importance of asexual and sexual reproduction to their growth and survival.
Delineate the impact of biotechnology on our society.
Describe the basic processes involved in the production of recombinant DNA.
Discuss examples of current uses of recombinant DNA technology in the agricultural and pharmaceutical industries.
Discuss the techniques of genetic screening.
Consider the implications of genetic screening of adults, children, and fetuses.
Discuss the application of population genetics to the study of evolution.
Describe the concepts of the deme and the gene pool.
Consider the Hardy-Weinberg principle.
Describe the factors which influence genetic drift.
Consider the relevance of the gene pool and the idea of mutations to the concept of evolution which will be studied later in unit 5.

units.name: Animal Systems
factorsEmphasized: D8 limitations of science and technology
D11 science, technology, and other realms
F1 longing to know and understand

items.text: To promote both intuitive, imaginative thought and the ability to evaluate ideas, processes, experiences, and objects within the context of the study of biological systems.
To enable students to understand and use the vocabulary, structure and forms of expression which characterize the study of biology.
To develop students' abilities to meet their own learning needs.
To support students in coming to a better understanding of the personal, moral, social, and cultural aspects of the study of life.
To develop students' appreciation of the value and limitations of technology within society.
To provide opportunities for students' active involvement in decision-making related to technological developments.
Describe how nutrients and oxygen are moved to the body cells.
Review the principles of diffusion and active transport.
Contrast passive transport systems, as in the cnidaria, with active transport systems, such as the human blood circulation system.
Compare open circulation systems, as in the grasshopper, with the closed systems of vertebrates.
Compare the efficiencies of hearts with one, two, three, and four chambers.
Describe the blood circulation pattern and vessels in the mammalian systems.
Explain the functioning of the human circulation system.
Describe the functions of the heart, lungs, kidneys, and liver in the circulation system.
Describe the ABO and Rh typing systems for human blood.
Consider the role of the blood in the immune system and the effect of the human immunodeficiency virus on the T4 cells of the blood.
Research the use of artificial hearts, heart transplants, the and circulation machines used during open-heart surgery.
Discuss respiration by relating the activity to the physical structure like the lungs and blood and the cells fed by the blood.
Describe the functions and functioning of nervous systems.
Describe the structure of a neuron.
Explain how neurons transmit impulses within and between themselves.
Compare the complexity of nervous systems in the planaria, earthworm, and human.
Contrast the functions of the central nervous system and the peripheral nervous system in humans.
Compare the structure of the brains of reptiles and humans.
Explain how the human endocrine system influences body development and maintenance.
Describe the general structure of hormones.
Describe the influence of the pituitary gland on body processes and on other glands.
Discuss the relationship between insulin and the body's control of blood sugar levels in the two forms of diabetes.
Outline the functions of hormones produced by several other glands.
Compare reproductive strategies among animal phyla.
Contrast the advantages and disadvantages of asexual reproduction with those of sexual reproduction.
Compare external fertilization with internal fertilization.
Describe fertilization in the earthworm.
Compare the amniotic egg of reptiles and birds with the structures which form in the uterus of a pregnant mammal.
Describe the production of semen in humans.
Describe the human female reproductive cycle from ovulation to either menstuation or implantation.
Trace the major developmental events from implantation of a fertilized egg to the birth of a human baby.
Identify the biofeedback mechanisms which are important in the regulation of the female reproductive cycle.
Describe how the use of the hormones found in birth control pills alters the reproductive cycle.
Discuss the relationship between the diet and health of the mother and the development of the fetus.

Investigate some technologies related to reproduction, such as in vitro fertilization, use of fertility drugs, birth control, amniocentesis, genetic screening of prospective parents, sperm banks, etc.

units.name: Evolution
factorsEmphasized: D11 science, technology, and other realms
F3 search for data and their meaning

items.text: To develop an understanding of how knowledge is created, evaluated, refined, and changed within biology.
To enable students to understand and use the vocabulary, structures and forms of expression which characterize the study of science.
To support the development of a positive disposition to life-long learning.
To support students in treating themselves and others with respect.
Explain how the evolutionary theory unifies biology.
Describe how individual variations are produced.
Discuss the action of natural selection on individuals, populations, and species.
Explain how Darwin's observations led to his inferences about evolution.
Compare the development of theories of evolutionary change (some examples - Lamarck, De Vries, Weisman).
Recognize evidence of evolution.
Discuss the use of the fossil record in the creation of lines of phylogeny.
Examine data from comparative anatomy and comparative embryology.
Describe instances of evolution documented in earth history.
Discuss the theory of continental drift and how that might have contributed to the changing variety of organisms that exist today. Where possible consider examples.
Examine broad climatic changes during the earth's history (ice ages, melting of the ice caps) and consider how these changes may have contributed to the changing organisms.
Examine the effects of migration and mutations on evolutionary change.
Discuss how evolution proceeds.
Compare gradualism and punctuated equilibrium.
Discuss the implications of the Hardy-Weinberg principle.
Describe the role of isolation in speciation.
Identify both pre-mating and post-mating barriers to recombination and reproduction.
Consider the speciation and development of humans.

notes: Structure as printed: for each core unit, 'Factors of Scientific Literacy Which Should be Emphasized' (codes defined in the guide's Dimensions of Scientific Literacy section; kept as printed in factorsEmphasized), 'Common Essential Learnings Foundational Objectives' (code = CEL abbreviation as printed), and 'Biology Foundational and Learning Objectives' (bold numbered foundational objectives, decimal-numbered learning objectives).
The guide says learning objectives 'can be selected from those listed or can be developed by the teacher and students' (p. 3 printed); they are not all mandatory.
Biology 20: 4 core units (78 h minimum) + optional time; Biology 30: 5 core units + optional time. Optional Plans pages list suggestions only (no objectives) and are not extracted.
The guide states 'Biology 20 is not a prerequisite for Biology 30' (printed p. 82).
Codes like '1' and '1.1' restart in every unit; they are only unique within a unit (and level).

Text extracted with pdfjs-dist (legacy build) from a 1992 WordPerfect-generated PDF; two-column pages split at x=300. Bullet glyphs (WPTypographicSymbols '!') and box-drawing dashes (WPBoxDrawing ')') were mapped to '•' and '—'.

Status on the site (2026-11-21): the course page has no notice that the guide is superseded; it offers only the PDF (its 'Outcomes & Indicators' page is empty). The course is reachable only through the site's search list: the 'Browse by Subject' → Sciences menu lists Science 10, Computer Science 20/30, Environmental Science 20, Health Science 20, Physical Science 20, Biology 30, Chemistry 30, Physics 30 and Earth Science 30, and not the 1992 'Biology/Chemistry/Physics 20, 30' entries.

The renewed Health Science 20 curriculum (CurriculumFile?id=74, Health_Science_20_2020.pdf, p. 3) says: 'Saskatchewan has developed science courses at Grade 11 that provide students with opportunities to learn core biology, chemistry and physics disciplinary ideas within interdisciplinary contexts.' and 'The current credit requirements for graduation from Grade 12 are one 10-level credit and one 20-level credit in science.' Neither document names Biology 20, Chemistry 20 or Physics 20 or says they were withdrawn; the authoritative list of courses in effect is the Registrar's Handbook for School Administrators (not checked).
The 30-level parts of this guide are superseded on the site by the renewed Biology 30 / Chemistry 30 / Physics 30 (ids 68, 69, 72), which have outcomes in sk.json.
